newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen leader renames capital for Dudayev.
newsitem.headline: Chechen leader renames capital for Dudayev.

text.p: Chechen leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev on Thursday renamed the regional capital Grozny in honour of late separatist president Dzhokhar Dudayev, less than a week before post-war elections in Chechnya.

"Expressing the will of the Chechen people, in the name of the great and merciful Allah, I decree that the capital Grozny is renamed Dzhokhar-Ghala," Yandarbiyev told a crowd of 5,000 people gathered amid the charred ruins of the city centre.
Dzhokhar-Ghala means City of Dzhokhar.
"The new name is to be immediately put into use into all spheres of government life," Yandarbiyev said, reading from the order.
On hearing the surprise announcement, the crowd punched the air in cries of of "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest) and "Dzhokhar", waving green and red flags and portraits of the late leader.

It was not clear how the decision would be greeted in Moscow, which fought a 21-month military campaign to try to crush the separatists before agreeing in August to withdraw its troops from the region ahead of the January 27 elections.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov expressed Moscow's concerns about fairness of preparations for the poll in a telephone conversation with the head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Petersen, on Thursday, a ministry spokesman said.
Moscow has objected to the Chechens' refusal to allow voting among refugees in other parts of Russia. Some politicians have accused the OSCE of promoting separatism, charges it denies.
Some observers say these concerns may lead Moscow to refuse to recognise the poll, in which all the candidates are set on independence from the Russian Federation.
The announcment renaming Grozny was made at a ceremony to mark Dudayev being given the posthumous title of Generalissimo by the Chechen parliament earlier this week.
Yandarbiyev, acting leader since Dudayev was reported killed in a 1996 rocket attack, has based his campaign on convincing voters he is the charismatic Dudayev's natural successor.
But the bearded poet faces a struggle to hold on to power in Chechnya's January 27 presidential elections. A 63-member parliament will be chosen on the same day.

Former Chechen chief commander Aslan Maskhadov, who also attended the ceremony, is widely believed to be the front-runner. But field commander Shamil Basayev is thought by some observers to be gaining ground. Wartime propaganda guru Movladi Udugov is the only other serious contender in a field of 16.

Yandarbiyev read out what he said were appeals from Chechen voters calling for the candidates to unite around a single figure. Many people have expressed dismay that the campaign has smashed wartime solidarity between top pro-independence leaders.
Some in the crowd shouted "No to elections" and implored other candidates to back Yandarbiyev to minimise further splits.
The hopefuls have said they may meet again to discuss a possible unity candidate, but previous talks have failed.
A Reuter straw poll of about 150 likely voters in Grozny showed Maskhadov with more than 55 percent of the vote. Basayev was a distant second and Yandarbiyev way behind in third place.

Dudayev, a former Soviet air force general, declared the oil-rich Moslem republic independent in 1991. In death, he has assumed virtual god-like status among many Chechens, some of whom say they are sure he is alive.

Hardline separatist Salman Raduyev, who led a bloody hostage-taking raid on the Russian town of Kizlyar in 1996, told the crowd that the elections would only be for "acting president" because Dudayev was still alive.
"Those who say Dzhokhar is dead are just spreading lies. Presidents may come and go but there is only one Dzhokhar," shouted Raduyev, wearing red sunglasses.
Much of Grozny, once a thriving oil-refining centre of 400,000 people, was largely reduced to rubble during the war, in which tens of thousands of people died.

Grozny, which means "threatening" or "menacing" in Russian, was established as a riverbank fortress in 1817 by Tsarist Cossack armies driving southward towards the snow-capped Caucasus mountains in an effort to colonise the area.
